1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4.strategy: Fights for d5 from the flank without occupying the centre, and keeps both a central break with d4 and a kingside fianchetto available. White waits to see how Black sets up, and many different structures can arise by transposition. The cost is that no pawn stands in the centre yet, so Black chooses how to meet it.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop on g2, where it bears on e4 and d5 along the long diagonal, and keeps White's central plans open. White castles early and builds from a safe king, which usually means a closed, strategic game. The cost is that the centre is left to Black, who can occupy it at once with ...d5.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.d4.strategy: Occupies the centre with a pawn and turns the game into a queen's pawn opening with the knight already on f3. White takes space and opens the c1-bishop, and Black must decide between contesting the centre at once and setting up from a distance. The early knight rules out set-ups that need the f-pawn on f3.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3.name: Nimzowitsch–Larsen Attack
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3.background: Named after Aron Nimzowitsch, who experimented with 1.b3 in the 1920s and 1930s and more often used the order 1.Nf3 d5 2.b3, and Bent Larsen, who played 1.b3 frequently from 1968 to 1972.
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3.strategy: Prepares Bb2, which aims along the long diagonal at e5 and the knight on f6, and keeps the central pawns flexible. White lets Black take the centre and plans to undermine it later, in the manner of a flank opening. The cost is a slower claim on the centre, so Black can develop comfortably.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.e3.name: Zukertort Opening: Quiet System
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.e3.strategy: Opens the f1-bishop and supports a later d4. It is solid but slow, and once d4 follows, the e3-pawn shuts in the c1-bishop while Black is free to take space in the centre.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.d3.strategy: Supports e4 and opens the c1-bishop, but it claims no space. It is sound but modest, and White's game stays passive until e4 can be played.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c3.strategy: Supports a later d4 and opens the d1–a4 diagonal for the queen, but it develops nothing and takes c3 from the queen's knight. It puts no pressure on Black's set-up, which can develop freely.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops the second knight and watches e4 and d5 without committing a pawn. It blocks the c-pawn, so English set-ups with c4 are off for now, and Black takes the centre at once and can gain more space by chasing the knight.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.a3.strategy: Prepares b4 and keeps a black bishop off b4, but does nothing for the centre or development. White is still waiting while Black takes space.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.a4.strategy: Gains queenside space on the rim, but spends a tempo on a pawn move that does nothing for the centre or development.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b4.strategy: Advances the b-pawn where nothing defends it: after 2...e6 the f8-bishop attacks it, and White must spend another tempo on saving it or give it up to ...Bxb4. The advance also weakens c3 and leaves the queenside thin.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.h3.strategy: Takes g4 from a black knight or bishop, but spends a tempo on a rim pawn the position does not yet call for while White still has to develop.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.h4.strategy: Gains kingside space and prepares h5, but loosens the kingside for no concrete gain and does nothing for the centre or development.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.Rg1.strategy: Supports a later g4 and g5, but gives up the right to castle kingside and puts the rook on a closed file, so White's king stays in the middle.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.Na3.strategy: Develops the knight to the rim, where it eyes b5 and c4 but guards nothing in the centre and blocks the a-pawn. Black's ...d5 also covers c4, and the knight stays out of play.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.Ng5.strategy: Moves the knight a second time to attack h7 and f7, both of which are defended. After 2...h6 it has to go back to f3 or h3, and Black gains time to take the centre.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.Nh4.strategy: Moves the knight a second time, to the rim, where it watches f5 and g6 but does nothing for the centre. The knight is out of play while Black develops.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.Ne5.strategy: Centralises the knight too early: 2...d6 attacks it and it must retreat, so White spends two moves for nothing while Black gains central space and opens the c8-bishop.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.Nd4.strategy: Centralises the knight, but ...e5 or ...c5 attacks it at once and it must retreat, while Black gains central space with a tempo.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.Ng1.strategy: Returns the knight to its starting square and undoes the first move, giving Black a free tempo with the knight already on f6. Black takes the centre at once while White has to start over.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.e4.strategy: Leaves the e4-pawn undefended, so 2...Nxe4 wins it. White's lead in development is doubtful compensation, and Black keeps an extra pawn in a sound position.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g4.strategy: Hangs a pawn: nothing defends g4, since the knight on f3 blocks the queen's diagonal, so 2...Nxg4 wins it. White's rook can then hit the knight, but it simply retreats and Black keeps the extra pawn.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.a4 g6.strategy: Ignores White's flank pawn move and prepares the kingside fianchetto, so the bishop on g7 will bear on the long diagonal. The advance of the a-pawn has done nothing for White's centre or development, so Black can develop at ease and keep every set-up open.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.a4 d5.strategy: Takes the centre at once. White's flank advance has done nothing for the centre or development, so Black occupies the key squares with a pawn, gains space and can develop the pieces comfortably in any set-up.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.a4 c5.strategy: Takes control of d4 from the flank, so White cannot build a pawn centre there without a trade. Black gains queenside space and a flexible structure, while White's a4 has done little to meet it.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.a4 g6 3.b4.name: Zukertort Opening: Myers Polish Attack
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.a4 g6 3.b4.strategy: Adds a second flank pawn advance before the centre or the pieces are looked after. It grabs queenside space and prepares a bishop on b2, but the pawns on a4 and b4 can only be defended by pieces, and the long diagonal stands open for Black's fianchettoed bishop until White's own bishop arrives.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.a4 g6 3.d4.strategy: Claims the centre with a pawn backed by the knight, the principled answer to the fianchetto. The extra a4 does no harm and gives some queenside space, and White can build a classical centre while Black attacks it from a distance.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.a4 g6 3.c4.strategy: Takes the d5 square and gains queenside space without yet committing the centre pawns. White plays for a flexible, positional game, accepting that Black may occupy the centre first and then trying to undermine it.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.a4 g6 3.g3.strategy: Mirrors Black's fianchetto and prepares a quick castle, a safe and flexible set-up that keeps both central pawn advances in reserve. White does not claim the centre at once and plays the opening as a slow positional fight.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 d5.strategy: Takes the centre at once and, together with the f6-knight, makes it hard for White to achieve e4. The b2-bishop will bite on a solid pawn centre that White has to undermine, while Black develops in a straightforward way. The cost is some flexibility, since the d-pawn is committed early.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 g6.strategy: Answers White's fianchetto with one of its own: the g7-bishop will challenge the b2-bishop on the long diagonal. The set-up is flexible and keeps ...c5 available, but until Black castles the g7-bishop is undefended, so a careless move of the f6-knight can drop it to Bxg7.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 e6.strategy: Opens the diagonal for the f8-bishop and keeps the choice of set-up open, from a classical centre to a Queen's Indian style fianchetto. The price is a c8-bishop that stays shut in behind the e6-pawn until Black frees it.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 c5.strategy: Contests d4 at once, answering White's flank play with a strike at the centre, and keeps the pawn set-up flexible. The game tends towards symmetrical English-style structures, quiet and manoeuvring, where neither side commits early.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 b6.strategy: Copies White's set-up: the c8-bishop will meet the b2-bishop on the long diagonal, in Queen's Indian style. The structure is solid but somewhat passive, since Black has little quick counterplay and mostly reacts to White's plan.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece and eyes d4 and e5, but the knight blocks the c-pawn and commits itself before Black's structure is clear. Once Bb2 is played, ...e5 would leave the pawn attacked twice and defended once, so Black has to prepare it first.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 d6.strategy: Prepares to take space in the centre or to fianchetto the king's bishop. The move is modest: it does not contest e4 as ...d5 does, and White develops freely.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with a Slav-style pawn pair and keeps the c8-bishop free. It is solid but slower than ...d5 at once and takes c6 away from the b8-knight, so White gets time to develop.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 a6.strategy: Spends a tempo on a flank pawn that neither fights for the centre nor develops a piece, and prepares a later ...b5. Nothing punishes it at once, but White takes the lead in development.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 a5.strategy: Prepares ...a4 against the b3-pawn, but spends a tempo on the flank while the centre is uncontested, and the pawn can no longer cover b5 or b6. Harmless, but White develops undisturbed.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 b5.strategy: Grabs queenside space, but the pawn stands unprotected on the f1-bishop's diagonal, so after e3 or e4 Black needs ...a6 or ...c6 to hold it. Sound enough, but development falls a move behind.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 h6.strategy: Takes g5 from the f3-knight, though nothing threatens there yet. A tempo on a rook's pawn while the centre is uncontested, so White goes on developing, but it costs very little.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 h5.strategy: Gains space on the kingside and gives the f6-knight the g4 square, now supported by the pawn, but develops nothing, and ...h6 is no longer there to cover g5. White simply goes on developing.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, aiming at b4 or c5, without doing anything for the centre. Once e3 opens the f1-bishop's diagonal, Bxa6 bxa6 would double Black's a-pawns.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 Ng8.strategy: Retreats the only developed piece to its starting square and undoes the single useful move Black has made. White gains two tempi and develops at leisure.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 Ng4.strategy: Sends the knight to a square where h3 chases it away at once; …Ne5 hangs to Nxe5, so it has to retreat to f6 or h6, and White has gained a tempo with h3.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 Nh5.strategy: Places the knight on the rim to reach f4, but g3 takes that square away and leaves f6 as its only safe square, while the move does nothing for the centre or for development.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 Ne4.strategy: Centralises the knight too early: d3 kicks it at once and White gains a free move, since the retreat to c5 runs into b4 and the one to d6 blocks the d-pawn.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 Nd5.strategy: Puts the knight on a square where e4 or c4 hits it with tempo; White then builds a broad pawn centre, while Black's knight has spent three moves and been driven back.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 e5.strategy: Hangs the e-pawn: 3.Nxe5 wins it because nothing recaptures on e5, and 3…Nc6 4.Nxc6 dxc6 only trades pieces without regaining the pawn.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 g5.strategy: Drops the g-pawn: the f3-knight takes it and nothing defends it, since the e7-pawn blocks the queen's diagonal. Black gets some central play with ...e5 for it, but White is a pawn up and Black's kingside is loosened.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 Rg8.strategy: Forfeits kingside castling and sends the rook to a closed file, achieving nothing in the centre or in development. White simply goes on developing while Black's king has lost its natural home.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 d5 3.Bb2.strategy: Completes the queenside fianchetto: the bishop looks down the long diagonal at f6 and the kingside, while the b3 pawn covers c4. White lets Black hold a pawn in the centre and plans to undermine it from a distance rather than occupy it, keeping the choice of pawn break for later.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 d5 3.e3.strategy: Opens the diagonal for the king's bishop and guards d4, a quiet and solid set-up. White keeps the choice between a central break and piece pressure on Black's centre open, and the queen's bishop can still develop on the long diagonal.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 d5 3.g3.strategy: Prepares a double fianchetto and quick castling, a safe but slow set-up. It does nothing against the d5 pawn yet and leaves Black time to finish developing and build the centre.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 d5 3.Bb2 c5.strategy: Strikes at d4 straight away, claiming queenside space and making a central advance hard for White. Black builds a pawn centre on d5 and c5 that White will try to undermine with piece pressure, so the game turns on whether that centre proves a strength or a target.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 d5 3.Bb2 g6.strategy: Mirrors White's set-up: the fianchettoed bishop will oppose the bishop on b2 along the long diagonal, while the d5 pawn holds the centre. Black chooses a solid, evenly balanced game over grabbing queenside space and keeps the c-pawn flexible.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 d5 3.Bb2 e6.strategy: Supports the d5 pawn with a second pawn and opens the king's bishop, a solid set-up. The cost is the bishop on c8, which is shut in for now, and Black accepts a passive-looking but resilient position while White undermines the centre.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 d5 3.Bb2 c5 4.e4.name: Nimzowitsch–Larsen Attack: Norfolk Gambit
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 d5 3.Bb2 c5 4.e4.strategy: A pawn offer in the centre: both ...dxe4 and ...Nxe4 win it, because nothing defends it. White hopes that the bishop's diagonal, which opens towards g7 if the f6-knight takes, and quick play against Black's centre will pay for it, but White has to justify the pawn.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 d5 3.Bb2 c5 4.e3.strategy: The natural developing move: it covers d4, the square Black's c5 pawn watches, and opens the king's bishop. Against pawns on d5 and c5, White plays for piece pressure and a well-timed c-pawn break, a calm way to undermine the centre.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 d5 3.Bb2 c5 4.g3.strategy: A second fianchetto and quick castling, a safe plan. It leaves the e-pawn at home and puts no pressure on Black's d5 and c5 pawns for now, so Black has time to build the centre: sound, but less direct.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 d5 3.Bb2 g6 4.c4.strategy: Challenges the d5 pawn at once, so Black has to resolve the central tension instead of simply developing. White fights for the centre with a wing pawn and a long-diagonal bishop rather than a pawn centre, and puts the c-pawn to work for queenside space.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 d5 3.Bb2 g6 4.e3.strategy: Opens the king's bishop and supports d4, a solid set-up that keeps both centre advances in reserve. White does not try to refute the fianchetto but builds calmly and fights for the centre with pieces and later pawn breaks.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 d5 3.Bb2 g6 4.g3.strategy: A double fianchetto that mirrors Black's set-up and prepares quick castling. Sound and safe, but slow: it puts nothing on the centre and lets Black organise the pawns at leisure, so White cedes the initiative.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 d5 3.Bb2 g6 4.c4 c6.name: Réti Opening: Anglo-Slav Variation, Bled Variation
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 d5 3.Bb2 g6 4.c4 c6.strategy: Defends d5 with a pawn, so a capture on d5 is met by ...cxd5 and Black keeps a pawn in the centre. It builds a solid wall of pawns behind which the g7-bishop will bear on the long diagonal against White's bishop, and keeps Black's structure free of weaknesses.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 d5 3.Bb2 g6 4.c4 Bg7.strategy: Completes the fianchetto and offers the d5 pawn: after cxd5 the knight cannot recapture, because ...Nxd5 uncovers the g7 bishop to Bxg7, so Black must castle first and then go after the pawn. Sound, but it asks for care.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 d5 3.Bb2 g6 4.c4 dxc4.strategy: Takes the c-pawn and gives up the centre pawn: after bxc4 White has an open b-file against b7 and can take the centre with pawns later, while Black has no pawn in the middle. Black wins nothing lasting and hands White the space.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b4 g6.strategy: Meets the flank advance with a plain fianchetto: the bishop on g7 will bear on the long diagonal that White's b-pawn has just left open. Black develops sensibly and lets White's early pawn advance prove itself, since the b4 pawn has no pawn support.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b4 e6.strategy: Opens the f8-bishop against the undefended b4 pawn and so punishes the advance. White must spend a tempo protecting it: after Bb2 Bxb4 and Bxf6 Qxf6 Black has won a pawn and the queen hits the rook on a1.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b4 d5.strategy: Takes the centre first and leaves the b4 pawn to prove itself: the flank advance has not helped White's centre or development, so Black occupies the key squares and develops comfortably. A solid, less ambitious choice than winning material.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b4 g6 3.Bb2.name: Sokolsky Opening: Zukertort System
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b4 g6 3.Bb2.strategy: Brings the bishop onto the long diagonal at once, where it faces Black's coming fianchetto and presses on f6. The b4 pawn gains queenside space but has no pawn behind it, so White commits to a flank game: a fianchetto duel in which White hopes to profit from the extra space on the wing.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b4 g6 3.g3.strategy: Fianchettoes the king's bishop first and heads for the same long-diagonal duel Black is preparing. The catch is the open a1-h8 diagonal: until the queen's bishop reaches b2, Black's bishop on g7 attacks the a1-rook as soon as the f6-knight steps aside.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b4 g6 3.a4.strategy: Adds a second queenside pawn move before the bishop is out, to cramp Black on that wing with the a- and b-pawns. Black is left free to claim the centre, so the space is worth only what White's pieces can later make of it.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b4 g6 3.c4.strategy: Takes d5 and b5 under control with a pawn and stakes out the queenside with two advanced pawns. The b4 pawn has no pawn behind it and Black's fianchettoed bishop will have the long diagonal to itself, so White has to bring the queen's bishop to b2 soon.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.Nc3 Nc6.name: Zukertort Opening
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.Nc3 Nc6.strategy: Mirrors White's development and aims at the centre: the knight eyes d4 and e5 while Black keeps all pawn set-ups open. Quiet and flexible, it asks White to declare a plan, since neither side has yet committed to a structure.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.Nc3 d5.strategy: Takes the centre at once and controls e4, the square White's e-pawn and knight would like. Black commits to a classical pawn on d5 that White will want to challenge with a pawn, so flexible manoeuvring gives way to a direct fight for the centre.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6.strategy: A flexible, solid reply: it supports ...d5 and ...c5 and opens the king's bishop, while Black's knights stay free. Black commits little and keeps every structure open, with a little less central control than an immediate pawn on d5.
